unit.unitOverview: You have been asking questions since Unit 1, one frame at a time. This unit gives you the system behind them, so you can build a question you have never been taught instead of reaching for one you have. It covers the wh- words and their word order, yes/no questions with their short answers, and the tags English adds to the end of a sentence when it wants agreement. It ends with a set of questions asked badly and the same questions asked well, because the difference is rarely grammar.

visual.lectureScript:
You have been asking questions since Unit 1, but always as fixed frames — where is the station, how much is it, do I have to. This unit gives you the machinery, so you can build a question nobody has taught you.
First, the wh- words. There are eight and you know most of them already.
Who asks about a person. What asks about a thing. Where asks about a place. When asks about a time. Why asks about a reason. How asks about a manner or a method. Which asks you to choose from a limited set. Whose asks about the owner.
Two of those are worth separating carefully. What and which. What is open — what do you want? Any answer at all. Which is closed — which do you want? Choose from these. If somebody offers you three options and you ask what, it sounds as if you were not listening.
And how is the busiest word in the list, because it combines with other words. How much, how many, how long, how far, how often, how old. Six questions from one word, and you have met all of them already in earlier units.
Now the word order, and this is the important part, because it is one rule and it covers everything.
A question in English inverts. The subject and the verb swap places compared with a statement.
Statement: You are ready. Question: Are you ready?
Statement: She can drive. Question: Can she drive?
But most verbs cannot invert on their own, so English puts in a helper — do, does or did — and inverts that instead.
Statement: You work here. Question: Do you work here?
Statement: She works here. Question: Does she work here?
Statement: You went yesterday. Question: Did you go yesterday?
You already know that last one from Unit 14. It is the same rule.
And when there is a wh- word, it goes at the front, and everything else stays exactly as it was.
Do you work here? becomes Where do you work?
Did you go? becomes Why did you go?
So the order is: wh- word, helper, subject, verb. Where do you work. Why did you go. How much does it cost.
That is the whole system. One rule, applied consistently.
There is one exception and it is worth knowing because it looks like an error. When who or what is the subject of the question, there is no inversion and no helper.
Who told you? Not who did tell you.
What happened? Not what did happen.
Compare with: Who did you tell? There the person is the object, so the helper comes back. Who told you — the person is doing the telling. Who did you tell — the person is being told. Both are correct and they mean opposite things.
Second pattern: yes/no questions and short answers.
A yes/no question has no wh- word. It just inverts, or uses the helper.
Are you ready? Do you work here? Did you go? Can you drive?
And the answer is not just yes or no. English adds a short answer, which repeats the helper.
Are you ready? Yes, I am. Not just yes.
Do you work here? Yes, I do.
Did you go? No, I didn't.
Can you drive? Yes, I can.
The pattern is: yes or no, then the subject, then the same helper that was in the question. And the rule for finding it is simple — whatever word came first in the question is the word you send back.
Why does this matter? Because a bare yes sounds abrupt in English, in a way that surprises learners. It is not rude exactly, but it closes the conversation. Yes, I do keeps it open. This is a small thing that makes a large difference to how you sound.
Third pattern: question tags. These are the short questions English adds to the end of a statement.
It's cold today, isn't it? You work here, don't you? She didn't come, did she?
The rule has two parts and both are mechanical.
First, the tag uses the same helper as the sentence would. If the sentence has is, the tag has is. If the sentence has no helper, the tag uses do, does or did.
Second, the tag reverses. Positive sentence, negative tag. Negative sentence, positive tag.
It's cold, isn't it? Positive sentence, negative tag.
It isn't cold, is it? Negative sentence, positive tag.
And what are they for? Mostly, they are not questions at all. They are invitations to agree. When somebody says cold today, isn't it, they are not asking. They are opening a conversation, exactly as in Unit 13, and the expected answer is yes, it is.
You can survive without ever producing a question tag. You cannot survive without understanding one, because they are extremely common and they change what the sentence is doing.
Go to Patterns.

readings.title: One Rule for Every Question
readings.passageScript:
English questions look like a long list of separate frames to be memorised. They are not. There is one rule, and once you have it you can build a question nobody has taught you.
The rule is inversion. In a statement the subject comes first. In a question the subject and the verb swap places.
You are ready becomes Are you ready?
She can drive becomes Can she drive?
But most verbs cannot swap on their own. English solves this by putting in a helper — do, does or did — and swapping that instead.
You work here becomes Do you work here?
She works here becomes Does she work here?
You went yesterday becomes Did you go yesterday?
Notice what happened in that last one. The helper took the past, and the main verb went back to its plain form. That is the rule from Unit 14, and it is the same rule, not a new one.
Then, if there is a wh- word, it goes at the front and nothing else changes.
Do you work here? becomes Where do you work?
Did you go? becomes Why did you go?
So the order is always: wh- word, helper, subject, verb.
One exception, and it looks like an error until you know it. When who or what is the subject — when the person or thing you are asking about is the one doing the action — there is no helper at all.
Who told you? What happened?
Compare Who did you tell? There the person is receiving, not doing, and the helper returns. Who told you and who did you tell are both correct, and they mean opposite things.

readings.title: The Same Question, Asked Two Ways
readings.passageScript:
Most questions that fail do not fail because of grammar. They fail because of how they are aimed.
Why is the bluntest word in English. Why didn't you tell me? is grammatically perfect and it asks the other person to defend themselves. The information you actually wanted — when they found out, what they thought — is now much harder to get, because they are explaining rather than telling.
The same question aimed differently: When did you find out? That asks for a fact. It gets one.
This is the general pattern. A question about a person's reasons puts them on the defensive. A question about facts, times and sequence gets you information. If you want to know why something happened, ask what happened first.
There are three small words that soften almost any question, and they cost nothing.
Just makes it smaller. Could I just ask about Thursday?
Actually softens a correction. Actually, I think it was Wednesday.
Possibly softens a request. Could you possibly check?
And there is one opening that is more polite than any of them. I was wondering whether — I was wondering whether you could check the time. It is longer than the request itself, which is exactly what makes it polite.
One more thing, and it is the one people find hardest to believe. If an answer does not answer your question, ask again. Most people accept an unrelated answer rather than repeat themselves, because repeating feels rude. It is not. Sorry, I meant the time rather than the day is a completely normal sentence, and asking twice is far less awkward than acting on an answer to a question you did not ask.

readings.title: Asked Badly, and Asked Well
readings.setting: The same person asking about a delayed order, twice.
readings.passageScript:
VERSION A

  "Why is my order late?"
  "There's been a delay at the supplier."

  "Why didn't anybody tell me?"
  "I'm not sure who was handling it."

  "So when will it come?"
  "It should be soon."

  "Is that definite?"
  "I can't promise anything."

  [Nothing usable was obtained.]

-----------------------------------------

  VERSION B

  "I was wondering whether you could
   check an order for me. It was due
   Tuesday."
  "Let me look. Yes - it's held at the
   supplier."

  "When did it leave them?"
  "It hasn't. It's still with them."

  "Right. What's the exact date they've
   given you?"
  "The 14th."

  "And who should I contact if it
   doesn't arrive on the 14th?"
  "Ask for Dana on this number."

  "Just to confirm - the 14th, and Dana
   if it's late. Is that correct?"
  "That's correct."

  [A date, a name, and a next step.]

grammar.title: The wh- question system
grammar.explanation: Eight question words and one word-order rule that covers every question in English. Once you have the order, you can build a question nobody has taught you.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
THE EIGHT WORDS
  who    a person       what   a thing (open)
  where  a place        which  a choice from a set
  when   a time         whose  the owner
  why    a reason       how    a manner or method

HOW COMBINES:
  how much, how many, how long,
  how far, how often, how old

THE ORDER — always:
  WH- WORD + HELPER + SUBJECT + VERB
     Where  do     you    work?
     Why    did    you    go?
     How much does it     cost?

THE HELPER COMES FROM THE STATEMENT:
  You work here    -> Do you work here?
  She works here   -> Does she work here?
  You went         -> Did you go?
  You are ready    -> Are you ready?  (be needs no helper)

THE EXCEPTION — who or what as SUBJECT:
  Who told you?        NOT who did tell you
  What happened?       NOT what did happen
  but: Who did you tell?  (person is the object)
grammar.workedExample:
You want to ask where somebody works.
1. Start from the statement: You work here.
2. Work cannot invert alone, so add the helper: Do you work here?
3. Put the wh- word at the front and change nothing else: Where do you work?
Notice that here disappeared, because where is now asking for it.
Now a past one. Start from You went yesterday.
1. Add the helper, which takes the past: Did you go yesterday?
2. The main verb went back to plain — that is Unit 14's rule, not a new one.
3. Add the wh- word: Why did you go?
And the exception. You want to know which person did the telling.
1. The person is the subject — they did the telling.
2. Subject questions take no helper at all: Who told you?
If you find yourself writing who did tell you, ask whether the person is doing or receiving. Doing means no helper.
grammar.commonMistake: Keeping statement order after the wh- word — where you work, why you went. The wh- word goes in front of a question, not in front of a statement. The other error is doubling the past: why did you went. And the third is adding a helper to a subject question: who did tell you, what did happen.
grammar.memoryTip: Wh- word, helper, subject, verb. Unless who or what is doing it.

grammar.title: Yes/no questions and short answers
grammar.explanation: A question with no wh- word. The same inversion rule applies, and the answer is not just yes or no — English sends back the helper.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
THE QUESTION — invert, or use a helper
  Are you ready?
  Do you work here?
  Did you go?
  Can you drive?
  Have you got a moment?

THE SHORT ANSWER — send back the helper
  Are you ready?      Yes, I am.
  Do you work here?   Yes, I do.
  Did you go?         No, I didn't.
  Can you drive?      Yes, I can.
  Have you got it?    Yes, I have.

THE RULE FOR FINDING IT:
  whatever word came FIRST in the question
  is the word you send back.

WHY IT MATTERS:
  A bare yes closes the conversation.
  Yes, I do keeps it open.
  This is small and it changes how you sound.
grammar.workedExample:
Somebody asks: Do you work here?
1. Find the first word of the question. It is do.
2. The short answer sends that word back, with the subject.
3. Yes, I do. Or negative: No, I don't.
Now: Are you ready?
1. First word is are.
2. Send it back: Yes, I am. Note that are becomes am, because the subject changed from you to I.
And: Did you go?
1. First word is did.
2. Yes, I did. Or No, I didn't.
That is the whole system, and it means you never have to think about which verb to use in the answer — the question already told you.
grammar.commonMistake: Answering with a bare yes or no. It is not rude exactly, but it closes the conversation in a way that surprises learners, and it makes a friendly exchange feel like an interrogation. The other error is sending back the wrong helper: Do you work here? — Yes, I am. The question said do, so the answer says do.
grammar.memoryTip: Whatever word came first in the question, send it back.

In every one, the word you sent back is the word the question opened with. That is the only decision, and the question makes it for you.
Number 1 is the one that changes shape: are becomes am, because the subject moved from you to I.

grammar.title: Question tags
grammar.explanation: The short question English adds to the end of a statement. Mostly these are not questions at all — they are invitations to agree. You must understand them; producing them is optional.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
TWO MECHANICAL RULES

  1  The tag uses the SAME HELPER
       It's cold,        isn't it?
       You work here,    don't you?
       She didn't come,  did she?
       You can drive,    can't you?

  2  The tag REVERSES
       positive sentence -> negative tag
       negative sentence -> positive tag

     It's cold,      isn't it?
     It isn't cold,  is it?

NO HELPER IN THE SENTENCE?
  use do, does or did
     You work here, don't you?
     She went, didn't she?

WHAT THEY ARE FOR:
  Usually NOT a real question.
  "Cold today, isn't it?" invites agreement.
  Expected answer: "Yes, it is."
grammar.workedExample:
Add a tag to: You work here.
1. Is there a helper in the sentence? No — work stands alone.
2. So the tag uses do. The subject is you, so don't you.
3. Is the sentence positive? Yes. So the tag reverses to negative.
4. Result: You work here, don't you?
Now a negative sentence: She didn't come.
1. The helper is didn't.
2. The sentence is negative, so the tag reverses to positive: did she.
3. Result: She didn't come, did she?
Two decisions each time, and both are mechanical: match the helper, flip the sign. There is nothing to judge.
grammar.commonMistake: Not reversing — it's cold, is it? That is a real question expressing surprise, not an invitation to agree, and it lands very differently. The other error is answering a tag as though it were a genuine question and giving a long reply; cold today, isn't it wants yes, it is, and nothing more.

4. You can drive, ____?
5. It isn't correct, ____?
6. They went yesterday, ____?
grammar.answerKey:
1. isn't it  2. don't you  3. did she  4. can't you  5. is it  6. didn't they
Check the sign in every one: 1, 2, 4 and 6 follow positive sentences so the tags are negative; 3 and 5 follow negative sentences so the tags are positive.
Numbers 2 and 6 had no helper in the sentence, so do and did were supplied. In 6, notice the tag is didn't they and the sentence keeps went — the past is marked once, in the sentence, and once in the tag, and never twice in the same clause.

writing.title: Writing 1 — Twenty questions about one thing
writing.promptAndInstructions:
Choose one thing you genuinely want to know about — a job, a course, a service, a place.
Write twenty questions about it.
Use each of the eight wh- words at least once.
Include at least four yes/no questions.
Include at least two subject questions with who or what and no helper.
Then mark the three you would ask first, and say why those three.
writing.modelText:
About a training course:
1. What does the course cover?
2. How long is it?
3. Where does it take place?
4. When does the next one start?
5. Who teaches it?  [subject question — no helper]
6. Which days is it on?
7. Whose budget does it come from?
8. Why is it only offered twice a year?
9. How much does it cost?
10. Do I have to apply?  [yes/no]
11. Is there a qualification at the end?  [yes/no]
12. Can I do it part-time?  [yes/no]
13. Did anybody from my team do it last year?  [yes/no]
14. What happens if I miss a session?  [subject question — no helper]
15. How many places are there?
16. When do I have to decide by?
17. Where do I apply?
18. Who should I ask about the cost?
19. What is the exact closing date?
20. Which of these is the most important to ask first?
First three: 19, 10 and 9 — the closing date, whether an application is needed, and the cost. All three could stop the whole thing, and the rest only matter if those three are answered.
writing.successCriteria: All eight wh- words used; at least four yes/no questions; at least two subject questions with no helper; correct word order in every question; three marked as first with a reason
writing.support: Write the questions in any order and fix the word order afterwards. Trying to do both at once slows people down, and the order is mechanical enough to check in one pass.
writing.extension: Rewrite any question that starts with why so it asks for a fact instead. Which ones became more useful?

writing.title: Writing 2 — One conversation, two ways
writing.promptAndInstructions:
Invent one situation where something has gone wrong and you need information.
Write the conversation twice, both sides.
Version A: use why questions and yes/no questions about intentions. Eight lines.
Version B: ask for facts, times, names and next steps. Twelve lines.
Version B must obtain at least three specific things Version A does not.
End Version B by repeating the arrangement back.
writing.modelText:
VERSION A
"Why hasn't my appointment been confirmed?"
"I'm not sure — let me see."
"Why didn't anybody call me?"
"I don't know who was dealing with it."
"Will it still happen?"
"It should do."
"Is that definite?"
"I can't really say."

VERSION B
"I was wondering whether you could check an appointment for me. It was booked for the 3rd."
"Let me look. Yes — it's showing as unconfirmed."
"What does unconfirmed mean here?"
"It means the letter hasn't gone out yet."
"When will it go out?"
"They go out on Fridays."
"So it would reach me about the 8th. What's the exact date of the appointment?"
"The 3rd of next month, at 2pm."
"And who should I contact if the letter hasn't arrived by the 10th?"
"Ring this number and ask for the booking team."
"Just to confirm — the 3rd at 2pm, letter this Friday, and the booking team after the 10th. Is that correct?"
"That's correct."
writing.expectedLength: Two versions, eight and twelve lines
writing.successCriteria: Version A uses why and intention questions and obtains nothing specific; Version B obtains at least three specific things — a date, a name or number, and a next step; Version B opens with a request rather than a demand; Version B ends by repeating the arrangement back
writing.support: Write Version B first. It is easier to write a conversation that works and then break it than to write a broken one and fix it — and breaking it shows you exactly which question was doing the work.
writing.extension: Underline every question in both versions. Count how many begin with why. The counts will not be close.

writing.title: Writing 3 — Read both versions
writing.promptAndInstructions:
Use the two versions in Reading 3. Write full-sentence answers.
1. What did Version A's questions have in common, and why did they fail?
2. What does Version B's first sentence do that Version A's does not?
3. Name the three things Version B obtained, and the question that produced each.
4. Why does Version B end by repeating the arrangement?
5. Rewrite Version A's second question so it would get a useful answer.
writing.modelText:
1. They were mostly why questions and yes/no questions about intentions, so every answer was a defence or a hedge rather than a fact. Four questions produced four non-answers.
2. It makes a request rather than a demand — I was wondering whether you could check — and it supplies the fact needed to act on it, that the order was due Tuesday.
3. An exact date, from what's the exact date they've given you. A named contact, from who should I contact. And a next step, from the same question — ask for Dana on this number.
4. Because it confirms the date and the name in one sentence and invites a correction while the other person is still there. An error caught then can be fixed; an error caught later cannot.
5. Instead of why didn't anybody tell me, ask: when was it flagged, and who was handling it at that point? That asks for a time and a name, both of which can be looked up.
writing.successCriteria: Five answers, each a full sentence; answer 3 names all three and matches each to its question; answer 5 replaces a why question with a request for facts rather than simply softening it
writing.support: Count the question words in each version before you answer. Version A is nearly all why and is; Version B is nearly all when, what and who. That count is most of the answer to question 1.
writing.extension: Write the two further questions you would ask in Version B if the supplier missed the 14th.

writing.title: Writing 4 — Correct the ten mistakes
writing.promptAndInstructions:
Every sentence has exactly one mistake from this unit.
Write each out correctly and say which pattern it came from.
1. Where you work?
2. Why did you went?
3. Who did tell you?
4. What did happen?
5. Does she works here?
6. Do you work here? — Yes, I am.
7. Are you ready? — Yes.  (you want to keep the conversation open)
8. It's cold today, is it?
9. You work here, aren't you?
10. She didn't come, didn't she?
writing.modelText:
1. Where do you work? (Pattern 1 — a question needs the helper, not statement order)
2. Why did you go? (Pattern 1 — did carries the past, so the verb goes plain)
3. Who told you? (Pattern 1 — who is the subject, so no helper)
4. What happened? (Pattern 1 — what is the subject, so no helper)
5. Does she work here? (Pattern 1 — the helper takes the -s, so the verb goes plain)
6. Do you work here? — Yes, I do. (Pattern 2 — send back the word the question opened with)
7. Are you ready? — Yes, I am. (Pattern 2 — a bare yes closes the conversation)
8. It's cold today, isn't it? (Pattern 3 — a positive sentence takes a negative tag)
9. You work here, don't you? (Pattern 3 — the sentence has no helper, so the tag uses do)
10. She didn't come, did she? (Pattern 3 — a negative sentence takes a positive tag)
writing.successCriteria: All ten corrected; each labelled with the right pattern; numbers 3 and 4 remove the helper rather than adding one; number 7 fixes the effect rather than the grammar
writing.support: Numbers 2 and 5 are the same error in two tenses — the helper took the marking and the main verb kept it too. In both, the fix is to make the main verb plain.
writing.extension: Numbers 3 and 4 look like errors and are the corrections. Write two more subject questions and two matching object questions.

activities.title: Practice 4 — Ask it better
activities.instructionsAndItems:
Each of these would get a defence rather than an answer. Rewrite it to ask for a fact.
1. Why didn't you tell me?
2. Why is my order late?
3. Why did nobody check this?
4. Why is this wrong?
5. Why hasn't anybody called me?

activities.answerSummary:
Model answers — yours will differ.
1. When did you find out?
2. Where is it now, and what date have they given you?
3. Who was checking it, and when was it last checked?
4. What should it say?
5. When was it last updated, and who is handling it?
6. What were the other options?
7. How is this normally allocated?
8. What would need to happen for it to be fixed, and by when?
Every rewrite asks for a fact, a time, a name or a next step. Every original asks somebody to justify themselves.

answerKey.answerOrGuidance:
Model answers — yours will differ.
1. When did you find out?
2. Where is it now, and what date have they given you?
3. Who was checking it, and when was it last checked?
4. What should it say?
5. When was it last updated, and who is handling it?
6. What were the other options?
7. How is this normally allocated?
8. What would need to happen for it to be fixed, and by when?
Every rewrite asks for a fact, a time, a name or a next step. Every original asks somebody to justify themselves.
Numbers 7 and 8 are the hardest because both originals are really complaints rather than questions. The rewrite works by finding the actual information underneath — how the allocation works, and what the path to a fix is.
